summary: A sedating, older (typical) antipsychotic used as an add-on in psychosis to reduce hostility, impulsive behavior and aggression. Not available in the United States, and it should not be used if you have liver problems.
description: Periciazine (Neuleptil) is an older (first-generation) antipsychotic that is more sedating and calming, with fairly weak antipsychotic effects. In practice, it is used as an add-on in psychosis when the goal is to reduce hostility, impulsive behavior and aggression, not as a treatment for schizophrenia on its own. It can cause sleepiness, low blood pressure, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble peeing (anticholinergic effects), movement side effects, including tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last), and rare but serious problems like dangerous heart-rhythm changes (QT prolongation, torsades), blood count problems, and a rare emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome). It should not be used at all if you have liver problems.
patient_summary: Periciazine (Neuleptil) is a sedating older (typical) antipsychotic used as an add-on in psychosis to help with hostility, impulsive behavior and aggression. It is usually not strong enough on its own for schizophrenia. The trade-off is side effects: sleepiness, dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, and possible movement symptoms. Rare but serious risks include dangerous heart rhythm changes, blood count problems, and a rare emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome). It should not be used if you have liver problems.

primary.context: Used as an add-on in psychosis when the main goal is to reduce hostility, impulsive behavior and aggression.

secondary.context: May not work on its own for schizophrenia and other types of psychosis; usually used as an add-on rather than the only antipsychotic.

off_label.context: Sometimes used for agitation in the context of psychosis when sedation and behavioral calming are the primary goals.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Sedation is a core effect with periciazine. Dosing is often split with a larger evening dose to reduce daytime impairment.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Lightheadedness on standing can happen, especially early on or after dose increases. Falls risk goes up if you’re sedated and your blood pressure drops.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble peeing (anticholinergic effects)
common_adverse_effects.notes: These can range from annoying to dangerous (eg, paralytic ileus, urinary retention), especially in older adults or people with BPH/glaucoma/low gut motility.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Stiffness, shaking or restlessness (movement side effects, EPS)
common_adverse_effects.notes: May include a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms (dystonia), and Parkinson-like stiffness and shaking. The risk may be higher with higher doses, with older (conventional) antipsychotics, and in younger people (especially males).
Weight gain and hyperglycemia/glucose intolerance have been reported. Monitor weight and labs over time.

serious_risks.risk: Dangerous heart rhythm problems, including QT prolongation (a change seen on an ECG), a dangerous heart-rhythm change (torsades de pointes), and ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia (very fast or chaotic rhythms from the lower heart chambers): may be life-threatening

A dangerous, near-total loss of white blood cells (agranulocytosis) and other blood problems, such as low white cells (neutropenia) or low platelets (thrombocytopenia), which affect clotting: stop and get checked urgently if suspected
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, rigid muscles, confusion, unstable heart rate, blood pressure or sweating. Get emergency help.
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can be permanent); the risk goes up the longer you take it and with other risk factors
Seizure: reported; risk higher in those with seizure history or lowered threshold
Cholestatic jaundice / hepatic injury: discontinue if jaundice occurs
Pulmonary embolism / venous thromboembolism: reported, including fatal events
Aspiration pneumonia risk in vulnerable people due to esophageal dysmotility/aspiration association

safety.black_box_warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Periciazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to periciazine, phenothiazine derivatives, or any component
Altered states of consciousness or comatose states, particularly due to intoxication with CNS depressants (eg, ethanol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids)
History of blood count problems, including a dangerous loss of white blood cells (agranulocytosis)
Patients at risk of angle-closure glaucoma
Patients at risk of urinary retention due to urethroprostatic disorders
Subcortical brain damage, with or without hypothalamic damage (known or suspected)

precautions: Heart rhythm risk: QT prolongation (a change seen on an ECG) has been reported rarely; life-threatening rhythm problems, including a dangerous heart-rhythm change (torsades de pointes), have occurred with this drug family (phenothiazines)
Blood problems: a dangerous loss of white blood cells (agranulocytosis), low white cells (neutropenia) or low platelets (thrombocytopenia) can occur; stop at the first signs and get checked urgently
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, rigid muscles, confusion, unstable heart rate or blood pressure; stop immediately and treat as an emergency

Movement side effects (extrapyramidal symptoms, EPS) and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last): muscle spasms (dystonia), a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), Parkinson-like stiffness and shaking; the risk rises with dose and other risk factors
CNS depression: can impair driving/operating machinery and can worsen with other sedatives
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can be associated with esophageal dysmotility/aspiration; higher risk with age
Falls: sedation + orthostasis + motor instability can raise fall risk
Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and trouble peeing (anticholinergic effects); the risk is higher in older or frail people
Metabolic/endocrine effects: weight gain and hyperglycemia/glucose intolerance have been reported; monitor
Venous thromboembolism: VTE including fatal pulmonary embolism has been reported
Eye effects: long-term use of this drug family can cause changes in the retina; avoid if you have glaucoma

interactions.interactant: CNS depressants (eg, alcohol, opioids, hypnotics, sedatives)
interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression, impaired alertness, higher fall risk; severe risk in intoxication states (contraindicated when altered consciousness/coma is due to CNS depressants).
interactions.action: Avoid combining whenever possible. Use extreme caution and close monitoring if unavoidable.

interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of QT prolongation and life-threatening heart rhythm problems, including a dangerous heart-rhythm change (torsades de pointes), especially with abnormal blood salts or heart disease.
interactions.action: Avoid high-risk combinations when possible. Correct electrolytes and consider ECG monitoring when clinically indicated.

interactions.mechanism: More dizziness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure) and fainting.
interactions.action: Start low, go slow, and monitor orthostatics in higher-risk people.

interactions.interactant: Other medicines that cause dry mouth, constipation and trouble peeing (anticholinergic medicines), especially several at once
interactions.mechanism: Worsened constipation/ileus, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion, temperature dysregulation.
interactions.action: Keep the total load of these medicines as low as possible; watch bowel and bladder function and thinking.

interactions.mechanism: Should not be used with spinal or regional anesthesia.
Significant drug interactions may require dose/frequency changes or avoidance.
interactions.action: Consult a drug interactions database for guidance specific to you.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mental status and alertness (sedation, confusion, delirium): every visit

Movement side effects (stiffness, shaking or restlessness): every visit; rechecked about 4 weeks after starting and after dose changes; a formal rating scale at least once a year (or every 6 months if at high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia (lasting involuntary movements): every visit; a formal rating scale at least once a year (or every 6 months if at high risk)
Vital signs (BP, orthostatics, pulse, temperature) and clinical signs of infection: as clinically indicated
Fall risk: evaluate regularly in people 60 and older or when clinically indicated
Weight/Height/BMI: every visit for first 6 months, then quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually (especially if metabolic risk)
Fasting plasma glucose/HbA1c: ~4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel: ~4 months after initiation, then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
CBC: check prior to initiation and then periodically (especially first 2 to 3 months); monitor for blood dyscrasia symptoms
Blood chemistries (electrolytes, renal function, liver function, TSH): as clinically indicated; liver function periodically with prolonged therapy

Signs of high prolactin: asked about at every visit until stable; prolactin is checked if you have symptoms (changes in periods or sex drive, breast growth in men (gynecomastia), breast milk leaking (galactorrhea), erection or ejaculation problems)
Ocular exam: as clinically indicated; particularly if symptoms occur or in higher-risk vision conditions

Blood sodium in older adults: checked closely when starting or changing the dose, because of the risk of low blood sodium (hyponatremia), sometimes caused by SIADH (a hormone problem that makes the body hold on to water)

special_populations.pregnancy: Taking antipsychotics in the last three months of pregnancy may raise the risk of movement symptoms and/or withdrawal symptoms in newborns (for example agitation, feeding problems, stiff or floppy muscles, breathing trouble, sleepiness, shaking). Reported outcomes range from settling on their own to severe.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known if periciazine is present in human milk. According to the manufacturer, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with periciazine.
special_populations.pediatric: Children ≥5 years and adolescents (psychosis): Initial 2.5 to 10 mg PO in the morning, then 5 to 30 mg PO in the evening; start lower and increase gradually based on effect and tolerance. To minimize drowsiness, use divided doses with a larger evening dose.
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid for behavior problems linked to dementia or delirium unless non-drug approaches have failed and there is a risk of harm. Antipsychotics are possibly inappropriate for adults 65 and over because of a higher risk of stroke, worsening thinking and death in people with dementia, and they can contribute to low blood sodium (hyponatremia), sometimes caused by SIADH (a hormone problem that makes the body hold on to water). If used for an appropriate reason (for example psychosis), the lowest dose that works is used and reviewed often, including trying to reduce or stop it when appropriate.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dosage adjustment provided in manufacturer labeling.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Should not be used if you have liver problems now or have had them in the past.

dosing.titration: Periciazine dosing is commonly split with a larger evening dose to limit daytime sedation. In psychosis, it’s described as adjunctive therapy when targeting hostility, impulsivity, and aggression. Dose increases should be gradual based on response and tolerability, and maintenance should aim for the lowest effective dose.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If periciazine is being used for a chronic psychiatric condition, switching to another treatment is generally preferred over stopping outright when side effects are intolerable or the medication isn’t working. If a patient insists on stopping (and it’s not an emergency), taper over weeks to months to reduce withdrawal reactions and to watch for relapse early. Monitor closely for prodromal symptoms of recurrence.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Periciazine (Neuleptil) is used in psychosis as adjunctive therapy when the main goal is to reduce hostility, impulsivity, and aggression. It’s not positioned as a solo medication for schizophrenia—think of it more like a “behavioral calming add-on” when someone needs more containment than their primary antipsychotic is providing.
items: {link:condition:psychosis:Psychosis} (adjunctive therapy): Targeting hostility, impulsivity, and aggression
Behavioral stabilization in psychosis: When sedation and reducing behavioral volatility are clinically important

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Periciazine is described for adjunctive use in psychosis to reduce hostility, impulsivity and aggression. It may not be effective on its own for schizophrenia and other types of psychosis, so the expectation is usually add-on benefit rather than primary antipsychotic control.
sections.metric: Adjunctive behavioral symptom control in psychosis
sections.clinical_details: Clinical use here is symptom-targeted: calming behavioral volatility in psychosis, often using its sedating profile. If the goal is full antipsychotic efficacy for schizophrenia, periciazine may be insufficient as a stand-alone option.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Contraindicated in liver dysfunction. Also: watch for QT prolongation/arrhythmias, blood dyscrasias, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and severe sedation/orthostatic hypotension.
sections.black_box: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Periciazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
other: Cardiac conduction risk: QT prolongation has been reported rarely; life-threatening arrhythmias have occurred with phenothiazines, including torsades de pointes
Blood dyscrasias: agranulocytosis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia can occur; stop at first signs and evaluate urgently
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability—stop immediately and treat as emergency
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia: dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism; risk rises with dose and vulnerability factors
CNS depression: can impair driving/operating machinery and can worsen with other sedatives
Aspiration risk: antipsychotics can be associated with esophageal dysmotility/aspiration; higher risk with age
Falls: sedation + orthostasis + motor instability can raise fall risk
Anticholinergic effects: constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention; risk is higher in vulnerable patients
Metabolic/endocrine effects: weight gain and hyperglycemia/glucose intolerance have been reported; monitor
Venous thromboembolism: VTE including fatal pulmonary embolism has been reported
Ocular effects: prolonged phenothiazine therapy can cause retinal changes; avoid in glaucoma
patient_counseling: If you feel faint when standing, slow down—stand up gradually and tell your clinician if it keeps happening.
Don’t drive or operate machinery until you know how sedating it is for you.
Call urgently for fever + stiffness + confusion, severe weakness, or uncontrolled shaking—those can be emergency warning signs.
Report new restlessness, stiffness, tremor, or abnormal movements early—those are often treatable if caught fast.
Constipation can become serious. Hydrate, add fiber, and tell your clinician if you go days without a bowel movement.
If you notice yellowing of skin/eyes (jaundice) or dark urine, stop and seek medical evaluation—liver injury is a serious concern and liver dysfunction is a contraindication.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Sedation, dizziness/orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, and movement symptoms are the big buckets. Rare but serious risks include arrhythmias (QT prolongation/torsades), blood dyscrasias, NMS, seizures, and tardive dyskinesia.
plain_language_list: Dizziness, especially when standing up (orthostatic hypotension)
Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention
Weight gain and blood sugar changes
Sexual side effects and prolactin-related symptoms (eg, gynecomastia, menstrual changes)

common.patient_note: Sedation is a core effect with periciazine. Dosing is often split with a larger evening dose to reduce daytime impairment.
Lightheadedness on standing can happen, especially early on or after dose increases. Falls risk goes up if you’re sedated and your blood pressure drops.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention)
common.patient_note: These can range from annoying to dangerous (eg, paralytic ileus, urinary retention), especially in older adults or people with BPH/glaucoma/low gut motility.
May include akathisia (inner restlessness), dystonia, and parkinsonism. Risk may rise with higher doses, conventional antipsychotics, and in younger patients (especially males).
Weight gain and hyperglycemia/glucose intolerance have been reported. Monitor weight and labs over time.

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias including QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation: may be life-threatening
Agranulocytosis and other blood dyscrasias (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia): stop and evaluate urgently if suspected
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability—medical emergency
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements; risk increases with duration and vulnerability factors
Seizure: reported; risk higher in those with seizure history or lowered threshold
Cholestatic jaundice / hepatic injury: discontinue if jaundice occurs
Pulmonary embolism / venous thromboembolism: reported, including fatal events
Aspiration pneumonia risk in vulnerable patients due to esophageal dysmotility/aspiration association

sections.intro: Significant drug interactions can exist, and dose or timing changes, or avoiding a combination, may be needed. Key interaction themes with typical antipsychotics include added sedation, combinations that prolong QT, and medicines that worsen low blood pressure or anticholinergic burden.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If periciazine is being used for a chronic psychiatric condition, switching to another treatment is generally preferred over stopping outright when side effects are intolerable or the medication isn’t working. If you want to stop (and it is not an emergency), it is tapered over weeks to months to reduce withdrawal reactions and to watch for relapse early. Early warning signs of relapse are monitored closely.
key_points: Avoid abrupt discontinuation unless stopping due to significant adverse effects.
Tapering is advised over several weeks to months to reduce withdrawal symptoms and rebound symptoms.

Withdrawal symptoms can include agitation, alternating warmth and chill, anxiety, sweating (diaphoresis), dyskinesias, GI symptoms, insomnia, irritability, muscle aches, tingling (paresthesia), psychosis, restlessness, runny nose, tremor and vertigo.
Relapse monitoring matters: watch for early/prodromal symptoms of psychosis recurrence during and after taper.
If changing antipsychotics, cross-titration and overlap strategies are commonly used; no single universal switching strategy is established.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Periciazine dosing is commonly split with a larger evening dose to limit daytime sedation. In psychosis, it’s described as adjunctive therapy when targeting hostility, impulsivity, and aggression. Dose increases should be gradual based on response and tolerability, and maintenance should aim for the lowest effective dose.

adult.psychosis_adjunct_initial: 5 to 20 mg PO in the morning, then 10 to 40 mg PO in the evening
adult.psychosis_adjunct_titration: Increase gradually based on response and tolerability
adult.psychosis_adjunct_maintenance: Reduce to the lowest effective dose once stable
adult.psychosis_adjunct_reduced_dose_option: Reduced doses may be considered: 2.5 to 15 mg PO in the morning and 5 to 30 mg PO in the evening
adult.administration: To minimize excessive drowsiness, administer in divided doses with the larger dose in the evening
adult.renal: No dosage adjustment provided in manufacturer labeling
adult.older_adult: Initial ~5 mg/day PO; increase gradually based on response and tolerability. Doses >30 mg/day in divided doses are rarely needed. In late-onset psychosis, lower-range adult dosing is generally sufficient. Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and there is risk of harm; consider deprescribing attempts to reassess ongoing need.

sections.simple_explanation: This medication is often dosed with a smaller morning dose and a bigger evening dose because sedation is common. The goal in long-term use is the lowest effective dose—enough to reduce behavioral volatility without flattening the person or causing preventable side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Periciazine has special considerations in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and older adults—especially due to sedation, falls risk, movement side effects, and the broader antipsychotic safety signals in dementia-related psychosis.
sections.pregnancy: Use of antipsychotic agents during the third trimester may increase the risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms in newborns (eg, agitation, feeding disorder, hypertonia, hypotonia, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Reported outcomes range from self-limiting to severe.
sections.lactation: It is not known if periciazine is present in human milk. According to the manufacturer, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with periciazine.
sections.pediatrics: Children ≥5 years and adolescents (psychosis): Initial 2.5 to 10 mg PO in the morning, then 5 to 30 mg PO in the evening; start lower and increase gradually based on effect and tolerance. To minimize drowsiness, use divided doses with a larger evening dose.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic therapies failed and there is risk of harm. Antipsychotics are potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65 due to increased risk of stroke, cognitive decline, and mortality in dementia, and they can contribute to SIADH/hyponatremia. If used for appropriate indications (eg, psychosis), use the lowest effective dose and reassess frequently, including deprescribing attempts when clinically appropriate.
sections.hepatic: Contraindicated (history of liver dysfunction; hepatic impairment is a hard stop).
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment provided in manufacturer labeling.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Periciazine (Neuleptil) is available in Canada in oral capsule and oral solution forms. Dosing is commonly split, with the larger dose in the evening to reduce daytime sedation.
items: Capsule (oral), Canada: Neuleptil 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg
Oral solution, Canada: Neuleptil 10 mg/mL (100 mL)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Periciazine is a phenothiazine (piperidine group) with sedative and relatively weak antipsychotic properties. It blocks subcortical dopamine receptors in the brain and can depress the release of hypothalamic and hypophyseal hormones.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Periciazine has a very specific role: add-on behavioral stabilization in psychosis, especially when hostility, impulsivity and aggression are the main concern and a sedating profile is useful. It may not be effective on its own for schizophrenia and other psychoses, so it is generally not a first-choice stand-alone antipsychotic. In older adults, it is generally avoided for dementia-related behavioral symptoms unless non-drug approaches fail and there is a risk of harm.

faqs.a: Periciazine is used as an add-on in psychosis to target hostility, impulsive behavior and aggression. It is not meant as a stand-alone schizophrenia medicine; it is more of an add-on when behavior swings need extra control.

faqs.q: Is periciazine available in the United States?
faqs.a: No. It is not available in the U.S.

faqs.q: Is periciazine a strong antipsychotic for schizophrenia?
faqs.a: Periciazine may not work on its own for schizophrenia and other types of psychosis. In practice, that means it is usually used as an add-on rather than the only antipsychotic.

faqs.q: Why is the larger dose often given in the evening?
faqs.a: Because sedation is common. Dividing the dose with a bigger evening portion can reduce daytime drowsiness while still providing the calming effect.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects people notice?
faqs.a: The main ones are drowsiness or sedation, dizziness (especially when standing up), dry mouth and constipation (anticholinergic effects), and movement symptoms (EPS) like restlessness, stiffness or shaking.

faqs.q: What are the serious risks I should know about?
faqs.a: Serious risks include dangerous heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation, torsades), severe blood count problems (like a dangerous loss of white blood cells (agranulocytosis)), a rare emergency with fever, rigid muscles and confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), seizures, and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last).

It should not be used by people who have liver problems now or have had them before. It also should not be used in coma or reduced consciousness from sedative overdose, in circulatory collapse, in people with a history of blood count problems or a dangerous loss of white blood cells (agranulocytosis), in people having spinal or regional anesthesia, or in certain high-risk glaucoma or urine retention situations, among other reasons on the label.

faqs.q: Can periciazine cause movement side effects?
faqs.a: Yes. Possible side effects include movement symptoms such as a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms (dystonia) and Parkinson-like stiffness, and tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last). Checks for these are recommended, including a formal rating scale at least once a year (more often if at high risk).

faqs.q: What monitoring should I expect if I’m taking it longer-term?
faqs.a: Checks commonly include: how you are doing and how sleepy you are at every visit; movement side effect checks (often every visit, with formal scales from time to time); weight and BMI early and regularly; blood sugar and cholesterol around 4 months after starting and then yearly; blood counts from time to time (especially early on); and blood pressure lying and standing when needed. In older adults, sodium checks may be considered because of the risk of low blood sodium (hyponatremia), sometimes caused by SIADH (a hormone problem that makes the body hold on to water).

faqs.q: How do you stop periciazine safely?
faqs.a: If it is not an emergency stop, tapering over weeks to months is recommended to reduce withdrawal reactions and to catch relapse early. Withdrawal symptoms can include agitation, anxiety, sweating, sleep problems, stomach and gut symptoms, shaking, restlessness, and possible return of psychosis, so close follow-up matters.

faqs.q: Is periciazine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Taking antipsychotics in the last three months of pregnancy may raise the risk of movement symptoms and/or withdrawal symptoms in newborns. For breastfeeding, it is not known if periciazine passes into breast milk, and the manufacturer does not recommend breastfeeding during treatment.
